articleSchema.headline: Why Postgres RLS Leaks Between Tenants
articleSchema.description: Postgres row-level security showed one tenant another tenant's rows under load. The policy was fine — the connection pool was handing out sessions with memory.
articleSchema.keywords: postgresql, row-level-security, node-postgres, multi-tenant, connection-pool, node-js

mainEntity.name: Does PgBouncer in transaction mode break this?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, unless every tenant-dependent statement runs inside one explicit transaction. In transaction pooling mode, PgBouncer can give each statement a different backend connection, so a session-level SET lands on one backend and your SELECT on another. Use the withTenant helper (set_config(..., true) inside BEGIN … COMMIT), or switch PgBouncer to session mode.

mainEntity.name: Should I run DISCARD ALL on every release?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's the simplest full reset, but a blunt one. It drops prepared statements, cached plans and sequence caches, so each reused connection pays a warm-up cost again — and it fails inside a transaction block. The leaner cleanup from the thread is ROLLBACK; RESET ALL; UNLISTEN *; SELECT pg_advisory_unlock_all();. If you rely on prepared statements, move the PREPARE calls into the pool's onConnect hook.

mainEntity.name: Why can't I write SET app.current_tenant = $1?

acceptedAnswer.text: The original question used exactly that, but SET is a utility command and Postgres only substitutes $1 placeholders in regular statements — pg gets back syntax error at or near "$1". The parameterised equivalent is SELECT set_config('app.current_tenant', $1, true). Never string-concatenate the tenant into SET; that's an injection point for switching tenants.
